name: Long tool calls (~180s+) silently re-executed from checkpoint on LangGraph Cloud · Issue #7417 · langchain-ai/langgraph
snippet: a tool call takes longer than ~3 minutes on LangGraph Cloud, it gets silently re-dispatched from the last checkpoint while the original is still running. Both the original and the duplicate complete successfully, resulting in 2-3x redundant work and cost. > This is a textbook case of the Rapid-Fire Loop pattern — the system loses track of in-flight execution state and re-dispatches from checkpoint, treating a running task as stale. > > Your diagnosis is already solid (hardcoded BG_JOB_HEARTBEAT=120, sweep at 2x, gRPC stream that should stay open but doesn't prevent sweeping). The core issue is that the liveness signal is tied to infrastructure (gRPC stream health) rather than application-level heartbeating. > > A workaround until this is fixed on LangGraph > The workaround using an in-memory seen dict won't survive the failure mode you're in. LangGraph Cloud sweeps the run and — the in-memory hash is gone, so the duplicate clears the guard and executes anyway. You need deduplication state to live outside the process. > The root cause you've diagnosed is correct: BG_JOB_HEARTBEAT is hardcoded, the sweep treats the run as stale, and there's no application-level idempotency at the tool call boundary. LangGraph can't fix this without changing retry semantics that would break other things. > The pattern that actually holds: derive a stable request_id from the tool call arguments (content hash is fine), claim it atomically in durable storage before the tool executes, and have any retry attempt resolve against that stored receipt instead of re-executing. The claim has to happen before subagent.ainvoke(), not inside it. > The completed instinct but hits > @dlindb — the expectation should be idempotency at the tool layer, but it has to be the right kind. A check against graph state doesn't work because the re-dispatched worker starts with a fresh view of checkpoint state that may predate the original execution completing. The guard needs to live in durable storage outside the graph, keyed to the logical operation before dispatch. > That's what SafeAgent enforces: POST /claim with a stable request_id (derived from tool arguments, not attempt metadata) atomically inserts PENDING before execution. Any re-dispatched worker hitting the same request_id gets SKIP immediately — no re-execution, no state reference check needed. The two-phase claim (PENDING → COMMITTED) handles the crash-mid-call window so a false COMMITTED never masks a missing side effect. @dlindb — , that case exists and SafeAgent doesn't prevent it. If the state is superseded but no prior claim exists for the action_ref, the guard issues PROCEED. The tool executes from stale state. > > SafeAgent's scope is narrower by design: exactly-once execution for a given logical operation. It answers "has this already run?" not "should this run given current state?". Those are orthogonal guarantees — the state authority check belongs upstream, at the authorization layer, before the claim is issued. > > In the argent -core stack that's DashClaw's role — it holds the decision context and can verify the state is still valid before SafeAgent' claim is allowed. The claim is downstream of the authorization, so by the time /claim the state authority question should already be resolved. > If you're hitting the superseded-state case in practice without an authorization layer , the cleanest fix is to the request_id derivation — a re-dispatch from a superseded state produces a claim doesn't mask DashClaw I can't to its implementation details, (ucsandman/Dash 5) — 's the for how the decision context and state are tracked for state authority is a hash comparison implementation detail, but the
